# (PART) Inferential Tests {-}

# The One-Sample t-Test {#t-statistic}

<div class="draft">Work in progress.</div>

## One More Function

- recap: small functions for mean, variance, SD, SE so far
- those pieces can also build a t-statistic: piece by piece, then check against R's own t-test
- the basic question:

<div class="summary-box">
How far is my sample mean from a comparison value, relative to the noise in the sample?
</div>

## A Score Example

- same ten values as last two chapters, mean 50

```{r score-data}
scores <- c(44, 47, 48, 49, 50, 50, 51, 52, 53, 56)
comparison_value <- 49
```

- comparison value = just the value we compare the sample against (e.g. scale midpoint, known benchmark, value from a previous study)
- same sample, two comparison values: first 49 (close to sample mean), later 46 (further away)
- keep an eye on what changes between the two and what stays the same

## The Equation

- the t-statistic:

$$
t = \frac{\bar{x} - \mu_0}{s / \sqrt{n}}
$$

- point out: bottom of fraction = SE equation from Chapter \@ref(standard-error):

$$
SE = \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}
$$

- so t = difference on top / SE underneath:

$$
t = \frac{\overbrace{\bar{x} - \mu_0}^{\text{difference}}}{\underbrace{s / \sqrt{n}}_{\text{standard error}}} = \frac{\bar{x} - \mu_0}{SE}
$$

- two halves pull opposite ways:
  - **the numerator:** bigger difference between sample mean and comparison value, bigger t
  - **the denominator:** bigger SE (spread in sample means), smaller t
- so t = how big the difference of interest is, *after* taking into account the uncertainty from sampling
- with our scores and comparison value `r comparison_value`:

$$
t = \frac{`r my_mean(scores)` - `r comparison_value`}{`r round(my_se(scores), 2)`} = `r round(my_t_value(scores, comparison_value), 2)`
$$

- `my_se()` already gives the bottom of the fraction, so the t-value needs only one new step: the division
- read as:

1. calculate the sample mean
2. subtract the comparison value
3. calculate the SE
4. divide the difference by the SE

## Build The Pieces

- every piece of the equation is something already built:

```{r t-pieces}
mean_score <- my_mean(scores)
se_score <- my_se(scores)

c(mean = mean_score, se = se_score)
```

- now put the pieces into the equation yourself: one line, subtract comparison value from mean, then divide by SE

```{r t-by-hand-exercise, eval=FALSE}
t_value <-
t_value
```

`r hide("Show a hint")`
Use `mean_score`, `comparison_value`, and `se_score`. Put brackets around the top of the fraction, so the subtraction happens before the division.
`r unhide()`

To two decimal places, t is `r fitb(c("0.95", ".95"))`.

`r hide("Show one solution")`
```{r t-by-hand}
t_value <- (mean_score - comparison_value) / se_score
t_value
```
`r unhide()`

- sign of t = which side of the comparison value the mean falls: positive above, negative below

## Your Turn: Write `my_t_value()`

- two inputs: values `x` and the comparison value
- recipe:

1. sample mean, using `my_mean()`
2. SE, using `my_se()`
3. subtract comparison value from mean, then divide by SE

```{r my-t-value-exercise, eval=FALSE}
my_t_value <- function(x, comparison_value) {
  mean_x <- 
  se_x <- 
  output <- 
  return(output)
}

my_t_value(scores, comparison_value = 49)
```

`r hide("Show a hint")`
The last blank is the same calculation you just wrote by hand, with `mean_x` and `se_x` in place of `mean_score` and `se_score`.
`r unhide()`

`r hide("Show one solution")`
```{r my-t-value-solution}
my_t_value <- function(x, comparison_value) {
  mean_x <- my_mean(x)
  se_x <- my_se(x)
  output <- (mean_x - comparison_value) / se_x
  return(output)
}

my_t_value(scores, comparison_value = 49)
```
`r unhide()`

- returns one number, the t-statistic; full t-test also reports df and a p-value (coming later)

The denominator of the t-statistic is the `r fitb("standard error")`.

## Check It Against `t.test()`

- R's version: `t.test()` from the `stats` package; as with every function so far, check ours against it
- first, the full output:

```{r compare-ttest}
t.test(scores, mu = comparison_value)
```

- the `t` in this output should match our function
- to check with `all.equal()`, pull the t-value out: `t.test()` returns a list of results, `$statistic` picks out t
- value comes with a label attached (`t`); `unname()` removes it, leaving just the number
- otherwise `all.equal()` reports the names differ, even though the numbers match

```{r compare-ttest-check}
t_result <- t.test(scores, mu = comparison_value)

c(mine = my_t_value(scores, comparison_value), R = unname(t_result$statistic))
all.equal(my_t_value(scores, comparison_value), unname(t_result$statistic))
```

- `TRUE` = your function reproduces the t-value from `t.test()`
- output also reports degrees of freedom (`df`), a p-value and a confidence interval
- one-sample test: `df` = sample size minus one, same $n - 1$ as in the variance

<div class="note">
**What about the p-value?**

- `t.test()` also reports a p-value
- it answers a question not yet asked: if there were no real difference, how unusual would a t-value this far from zero be?
- we build that ourselves in the companion book, [Demystifying Null Hypothesis Testing](https://demystr.github.io/nhst/): [Null Distributions](https://demystr.github.io/nhst/null-distributions.html) and [p-values](https://demystr.github.io/nhst/p-values.html)
- for now, focus on what the t-value itself tells you
</div>

## Your Turn: Write `my_t_test()`

- put the pieces together: one function returning a small table with t and its df

1. t with `my_t_value()`
2. df = number of values minus one
3. both into a table with `tibble()`

```{r my-t-test-exercise, eval=FALSE}
my_t_test <- function(x, comparison_value) {
  t <- 
  df <- 
  output <- tibble(t = t, df = df)
  return(output)
}

my_t_test(scores, comparison_value = 49)
```

`r hide("Show a hint")`
`t` uses `my_t_value(x, comparison_value)`, and `df` uses `length(x) - 1`.
`r unhide()`

`r hide("Show one solution")`
```{r my-t-test-solution}
my_t_test <- function(x, comparison_value) {
  t <- my_t_value(x, comparison_value)
  df <- length(x) - 1
  output <- tibble(t = t, df = df)
  return(output)
}

my_t_test(scores, comparison_value = 49)
```
`r unhide()`

## Check It Against `t.test()` Again

- `t.test()` keeps df under the name `parameter`
- to check both numbers at once: put R's t and df into a one-row tibble shaped like `my_t_test()`'s output
- as in Chapter \@ref(standard-error): `bind_rows()` stacks the two rows side by side, `all.equal()` compares the whole table

```{r my-t-test-check}
my_result <- my_t_test(scores, comparison_value)
r_result <- tibble(
  t = unname(t_result$statistic),
  df = unname(t_result$parameter)
)

bind_rows(mine = my_result, R = r_result, .id = "version")
all.equal(my_result, r_result)
```

- `TRUE` = own functions reproduce t and df from `t.test()`
- interpret: mean `r round(my_mean(scores), 2)`, comparison `r comparison_value`, mean sits `r round(my_t_value(scores, comparison_value), 2)` SEs above it

## A Second Comparison Value

- same sample against 46

```{r second-comparison}
comparison_value_2 <- 46

my_result_2 <- my_t_test(scores, comparison_value_2)
t_result_2 <- t.test(scores, mu = comparison_value_2)
r_result_2 <- tibble(
  t = unname(t_result_2$statistic),
  df = unname(t_result_2$parameter)
)

bind_rows(mine = my_result_2, R = r_result_2, .id = "version")
all.equal(my_result_2, r_result_2)
```

- point out: mean still `r round(my_mean(scores), 2)`, SE still `r round(my_se(scores), 2)`; only comparison value changed
- difference now `r round(my_mean(scores) - comparison_value_2, 2)` not `r round(my_mean(scores) - comparison_value, 2)`, so t is `r round(my_t_value(scores, comparison_value_2), 2)` not `r round(my_t_value(scores, comparison_value), 2)`

| Comparison value | Difference | Standard error | t |
|---|---|---|---|
| `r comparison_value` | `r round(my_mean(scores) - comparison_value, 2)` | `r round(my_se(scores), 2)` | `r round(my_t_value(scores, comparison_value), 2)` |
| `r comparison_value_2` | `r round(my_mean(scores) - comparison_value_2, 2)` | `r round(my_se(scores), 2)` | `r round(my_t_value(scores, comparison_value_2), 2)` |

- t = distance between sample mean and comparison value, measured in SEs
- mean nearly four SEs from the comparison value much harder to put down to noise than one about one SE away
- deciding how far is far enough = job of p-values; [Null Distributions](https://demystr.github.io/nhst/null-distributions.html) in the NHST book builds the null distribution they need from scratch, [p-values](https://demystr.github.io/nhst/p-values.html) turns it into p-values

Which part of the t-statistic changed between the two tests? `r mcq(c("the standard error", answer = "the difference between the sample mean and the comparison value", "the sample size"))`

- try a third comparison value: 55; predict the sign of t before running

`r hide("Show one solution")`
```{r t-sign-exercise}
my_t_test(scores, comparison_value = 55)
t.test(scores, mu = 55)
```
The t-value is negative because our sample mean is below 55.
`r unhide()`

## Try It On Real Data

- back to `sleep` from Chapter \@ref(standard-error)
- did the first drug add any sleep, on average?
- if it did nothing, population mean of `extra` = 0, so 0 is the comparison value
- run your t-test and R's:

```{r real-data-ch4}
drug_1 <- sleep %>% filter(group == 1) %>% pull(extra)

my_result <- my_t_test(drug_1, comparison_value = 0)
drug_t_result <- t.test(drug_1, mu = 0)
drug_r_result <- tibble(
  t = unname(drug_t_result$statistic),
  df = unname(drug_t_result$parameter)
)

bind_rows(mine = my_result, R = drug_r_result, .id = "version")
all.equal(my_result, drug_r_result)
```

- interpret: on average `r my_mean(drug_1)` hours more sleep, mean about `r round(my_t_value(drug_1, 0), 1)` SEs above 0
- whether that is far enough to rule out noise: [p-values](https://demystr.github.io/nhst/p-values.html) in the NHST book

```{r my-functions-after-2a-t-statistic, eval=FALSE}
# My statistics functions
#
# Add each function you build to this file, under the heading of the
# chapter you built it in. Later chapters load it with
# source("my_functions.R"), so every function here can be reused.
#
# Keep only the functions in this file. Run and check them in your
# exercise files, not here.
#
# Some functions return a tibble, so load the tidyverse before using them.


# PART I: BASICS AND SUMMARY STATISTICS ====================================


# From Equations to Code ---------------------------------------------------
my_mean <- function(x) {
  total <- sum(x)
  n <- length(x)
  output <- total / n
  return(output)
}

my_var <- function(x) {
  n <- length(x)
  mean_x <- my_mean(x)
  squared_distances <- (x - mean_x)^2
  total_squared_distance <- sum(squared_distances)

  output <- total_squared_distance / (n - 1)
  return(output)
}



# Spread and Standard Error ------------------------------------------------
my_sd <- function(x) {
  output <- sqrt(my_var(x))
  return(output)
}

my_se <- function(x) {
  n <- length(x)
  sd_x <- my_sd(x)
  output <- sd_x / sqrt(n)
  return(output)
}

my_summary <- function(x) {
  output <- tibble(
    n = length(x),
    mean = my_mean(x),
    variance = my_var(x),
    sd = my_sd(x),
    se = my_se(x)
  )
  return(output)
}

my_z_score <- function(x) {
  mean_x <- my_mean(x)
  sd_x <- my_sd(x)
  output <- (x - mean_x) / sd_x
  return(output)
}



# PART II: INFERENTIAL TESTS ==============================================


# The One-Sample t-Test ----------------------------------------------------
my_t_value <- function(x, comparison_value) {
  mean_x <- my_mean(x)
  se_x <- my_se(x)
  output <- (mean_x - comparison_value) / se_x
  return(output)
}

my_t_test <- function(x, comparison_value) {
  t <- my_t_value(x, comparison_value)
  df <- length(x) - 1
  output <- tibble(t = t, df = df)
  return(output)
}



# Covariance and Correlation -----------------------------------------------
```

## Where This Goes Next

- you have built a one-sample t-statistic entirely from your own functions:

<div class="summary-box">
values -> mean -> variance -> standard deviation -> standard error -> t
</div>

- one t-value tells us about one sample; two ways to carry on:
  - **Keep building.** Next chapter builds another test statistic from the same pieces; Part II keeps going like this, one statistic at a time
  - **Dip into the NHST book.** [Null Distributions](https://demystr.github.io/nhst/null-distributions.html) in [Demystifying Null Hypothesis Testing](https://demystr.github.io/nhst/) takes the t-value just built and simulates thousands of samples to find out what "far enough" means; [p-values](https://demystr.github.io/nhst/p-values.html) turns that into p-values; only needs the chapters done here so far; can come back to Part I afterwards
- either order works; not sure? keep building, come back to the NHST book once you have a few test statistics under your belt
